name: bluewater-12-nine-reviews
lines: You did three hundred jobs last year. Nine people said so.
Three hundred customers. Most of them thrilled. Nine reviews.
The company down the road has four hundred and twelve.
And tonight a stranger is choosing between the two of you. She's never met either one. All she's got is that number.
So let's fix the number.
Picture Ivy. I invented her, so don't go looking her up.
Ivy cleans carpets. Nine years. One van. And she is very, very good.
Here's a normal Thursday. A living room. A stain the customer gave up on two years ago.
Forty minutes later, it's gone.
I can't believe that's the same carpet. I'm telling everybody.
And Ivy says what you'd say. Thank you so much. Then she packs the van and drives to the next job.
Here's the part that stings. That customer meant every word.
And she told nobody. Not online, anyway.
Not because she's lazy. Because nobody asked her, and by dinner she was thinking about dinner.
Now it's Tuesday night, across town. Red wine. Cream carpet.
She types carpet cleaning, and two names come up.
Ivy. Four point nine stars. Nine reviews. The newest one is eight months old.
The other one. Four point six stars. Four hundred and twelve reviews. The newest one is from yesterday.
She calls the four hundred and twelve. She never even opened Ivy's page.
Ivy has the better score. It didn't matter. Nine looks like a hobby. Four hundred looks like a business.
Here's what that might cost. Say that search skips Ivy twice a week.
Say a clean is two hundred and fifty dollars.
That's twenty five thousand dollars a year, walking past the best carpet cleaner in town.
Those numbers are mine, not hers. She's invented. But run it with your own, and see what you get.
So here's the truth about reviews.
Your happiest customers are your quietest ones.
Happy people don't write reviews. Asked people do.
Three moves. You can start on your very next job.
Move one. Ask at the wow.
Not in an email next week. Right there, in the living room, the second she says I can't believe it.
Would you mind saying that in a Google review? It really helps a small business like mine.
That's the whole script. She already said the nice thing. You're just asking her to say it where it counts.
Move two. Make it one tap.
Google lets you make a link, or a little code she can scan, that opens straight to the stars.
Text her the link before you start the van. If she has to search for you, she won't.
Print the code on your invoice too. The next customer will find it by herself.
Move three. Make asking part of the job.
You don't decide whether to roll up the hose. You just do it. Asking goes on that list.
And count the asks, not the reviews. You can't control who writes one. You can control whether you asked.
Now two things you never do.
Never offer a discount for a review. Google's own rules ban it, and it isn't worth your name.
And don't ask only the ones you think loved you. Ask everybody. A real mix reads more honest than a perfect wall.
So. Six months later. Another Tuesday night. Another glass of red.
Same search. Same two names.
Ivy. Four point nine stars. Eighty seven reviews. The newest one is from two days ago.
This time she opens Ivy's page. And she reads the first review.
It says, I couldn't believe it was the same carpet.
Six months ago, that sentence was said out loud in a living room and it was gone by dinner.
Now it's doing Ivy's selling for her, at nine o'clock at night, while she's asleep.
I can't promise you the top spot on Google. Nobody can, and anybody who says they can is selling something.
What I can tell you is what a stranger sees when she looks you up.
So do this tonight.
Open your Google Business Profile and find where it lets you ask for reviews. Copy that link.
Then text it to the last three customers who said wow. Just three.
Ivy's number was nine. What's yours?
And if your Google profile needs more than reviews, that's work we do. The link's in the description.
